incidents.cause: The pilot's failure to maintain the glidepath and appropriate airspeed during landing in icing conditions, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall and a hard landing.
The pilot's failure to properly follow the manual landing gear extension procedure, resulting in a gear-up landing.
The pilot’s loss of directional control during landing flare resulting in substantial damage to the left wing.
The pilot’s improper checklist use, which resulted in an electrical malfunction and subsequent gear up landing.

The pilot's failure to attain a positive climb rate during an attempted missed approach in night instrument meteorological conditions that were at/near approach minimums, which resulted in controlled flight into terrain.
The pilot’s failure to maintain control of the airplane that resulted in an uncontrolled descent and overstress of the airframe during his recovery of the airplane.
The airplane’s in-flight collision with a bird.

The pilot’s failure to maintain clearance with the parked fuel truck while taxiing for takeoff. Contributing to the outcome was the pilot’s decision to park the airplane in the congested ramp area and his excessive taxi speed.
The pilot's descent below minimum descent altitude during the nonprecision instrument approach for reasons that could not be determined based on the available information.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during an attempted aborted landing in gusty crosswind conditions, which resulted in a runway excursion and an impact with a tree.
An inadvertent collision with a bird while on downwind in the airport pattern.
The student pilot's failure to maintain directional control during takeoff.
An inadvertent collision with a deer while landing.
An engine fire, which resulted from the overpriming of a hot engine.
A partial loss of engine power due to the formation of carburetor ice during descent for landing. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s failure to apply carburetor heat.
The student pilot's overpriming of the engine and the flight instructor's delayed remedial action, which resulted in an engine fire.

The in-flight fatigue failure of the crankshaft gear retaining bolt, which resulted in a total loss of engine power. The student pilot’s failure to maintain altitude during approach, which resulted in controlled flight into terrain. Contributing to the accident was the student’s distraction due to other traffic in the airport traffic pattern.
A loss of control during the attempted go-around, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall and impact with trees.

The pilot's inadequate preflight planning, which resulted in his attempt to take off near the airplane’s maximum gross weight in high-density altitude conditions that degraded the airplane’s takeoff and climb performance and resulted in an aborted takeoff and subsequent runway excursion.
A total loss of engine power during cruise flight due to piston fatigue cracking for reasons that could not be determined due to postfracture smearing damage.

incidents.op: WRONG BROS AVIATOR TRAINING SCHOOL LLC
incidents.cause: The pilot’s loss of directional control and long landing in gusting wind conditions due to his shoe getting stuck on the brakes.
The pilot's inflight loss of control for undetermined reasons.

A partial loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined because postaccident examination of the airplane revealed no mechanical anomalies that would have contributed to the power loss.
The pilot's failure to maintain adequate wing clearance while taxiing, which resulted in a collision with two unoccupied airplanes.
A loss of airplane control during takeoff for reasons that could not be determined due to the postaccident condition of the elevator control system.
The pilot's failure to maintain situational awareness during a turn which resulted in a loss of airplane control.

The AA-5 pilot’s failure to maintain separation from the 182T during approach and landing, which resulted in a ground collision during the landing roll. Contributing to the accident was the failure of the AA-5’s electrical system, which prevented the AA-5 pilot from communicating with other aircraft
The pilot’s failure to maintain airplane control while maneuvering in mountainous terrain. Contributing was mountain wave turbulence in the area.
The Cessna 172 flight instructor and student pilot's inadequate visual lookout and failure to maintain clearance from the stationary Cessna 182.
The in-flight collision with a bird.
The pilot's improper recovery from a bounced landing.
The flight instructor’s improper landing flare which resulted in a bounced landing and loss of control.
The pilot’s continuance of the GPS approach below the minimum descent altitude while landing in instrument meteorological conditions.
The pilot's improper landing flare, which resulted in a hard landing.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the crosswind landing.
A partial loss of engine power for undetermined reasons during an en route climb.

The pilot's failure to maintain aircraft control after inadvertantly encountering instrument meteorological conditions.  Contributing to the accident were the pilot's failure to obtain a weather brief and the severe weather conditions.

The pilot's delayed response to abort the takeoff, which resulted in an excursion and collision with a fence. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's failure to check the pitot tube for debris during preflight.

The pilot's failure to maintain pitch control during the takeoff roll during an attempted takeoff. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's selection of takeoff flaps after he began the takeoff roll.
The failure of the pilot to maintain directional control during the landing roll. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's improper use of a supplemental cockpit lighting during approach.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing, which resulted in a runway excursion and collision with an airport lighting system.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control of the airplane while landing with a crosswind.
The failure of the nosewheel steering pushrod, which resulted in a loss of airplane directional control and runway excursion.
The tug driver's inadequate control of the tug while maneuvering the airplane during pushback.
The cause of the right wing landing light switch fire is undetermined.
The flight crews failure to maintain clearance from the light pole while taxiing.
The pilot's failure to adequately compensate for a wind shift while on short final approach which resulted in a higher than normal sink rate and a tailstrike.
Failure of the tailwheel locking mechanism, which resulted in a loss of control during landing and a runway excursion.
The failure of the right brake master cylinder lock seal spring washer.
Loss of directional control to avoid a deer during landing, which resulted in a runway excursion and collision with a culvert.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll in cross wind conditions.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control while landing in a gusting crosswind, which resulted in a noseover. Contributing was the pilot’s lack of familiarity with the airplane.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during landing with a crosswind, which resulted in a runway excursion and subsequent ground-loop.
A fatigue fracture of the left main landing gear axle.

The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control of the airplane during the landing roll, which resulted in a ground loop and subsequent landing gear collapse. Contributing was the flight instructor’s delayed remedial action.
The pilot’s loss of directional control during landing in variable wind conditions.
The pilot's failure to maintain airplane control during landing resulting in a nose over.
A total loss of engine power for reasons that could not be determined during a postaccident examination of the airframe and engine.

The pilot's failure to maintain directional control while landing. Contributing to the accident was the pilot's decision to accept an advised runway rather than determine actual airport winds, which resulted in the airplane landing with a quartering tailwind.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll in crosswind conditions.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control of the airplane during an aborted landing, which resulted in runway excursion and collision with a ditch.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control after an attempted go-around, which resulted in a runway excursion and impact with terrain.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during the takeoff with a right crosswind.

The pilot’s decision to depart shortly after a landing helicopter, which resulted in an encounter with the helicopter’s wake turbulence and a loss of airplane control. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s impairment by his recent use of ethanol.
The pilot’s improper landing flare and subsequent loss of airplane control during a go-around when the airplane stalled and collided with the ground.
